title: Therapeutic remuscularization of the adult human heart

concept.text: Therapeutic remuscularization would repair an injured adult human heart by creating enough new, living heart muscle to restore a clinically meaningful amount of pumping capacity. The new cardiomyocytes—the cells that contract to generate force—would need to survive, contribute useful mechanical work, and coordinate their activity with the existing heart. Replacing lost myocardium is the regenerative goal described in the supplied review; successful human treatment is not established by that evidence.

Conceptual scope: the capability could be pursued by stimulating existing cardiomyocytes to produce additional muscle or by implanting replacement cells or engineered muscle. These routes belong to the same concept when they restore functioning myocardium within the patient's existing heart. An improvement caused only by temporary signaling from administered cells would not, by itself, demonstrate remuscularization.

significance.text: Myocardial infarction can leave irreversible fibrosis, loss of cardiomyocytes, and chronic cardiac dysfunction. A treatment that durably restored integrated, force-generating muscle and improved patient outcomes would make an important component of that injury therapeutically reparable. The revolutionary capability would be recovery of useful muscle in the damaged heart, extending beyond management of the consequences of muscle loss.

Conditional implications: successful repair could improve pumping capacity and reduce the burden of heart failure, potentially delaying or avoiding mechanical support or transplantation for some patients. Those consequences require clinical demonstration; producing additional cardiomyocytes does not automatically establish fewer hospitalizations, longer survival, or less need for replacement therapies. The supplied evidence does not quantify the eligible population or establish how its size would compare with populations served by replacement hearts.

Limits of the repair analogy: replacing muscle would not necessarily eliminate the cause of continuing injury. Extension from infarct-related muscle loss to dilated cardiomyopathy would depend on the underlying disease, the condition of the remaining myocardium, and control of ongoing damage. Transplantation also supplies working myocardium through whole-organ replacement, so it would be misleading to suggest that all existing treatments merely manage failure without providing muscle. Remuscularization specifically seeks to repair the existing heart.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a controllable way to generate and integrate enough new contractile myocardium to improve the injured adult human heart safely and durably. Adult mammals have largely lost the ability to replace myocardium through cardiomyocyte proliferation. The supplied review identifies manipulation of cardiomyocyte maturation and cell-cycle control as a foundation for regenerative strategies, while reporting progress in adult-animal models rather than an established human therapy.

Engineering synthesis: stimulating endogenous regeneration would require productive formation of additional cardiomyocytes, rather than treating a cell-cycle signal alone as evidence of new muscle. It would also require sufficient control over the location, extent, and duration of proliferation, followed by muscle capable of performing useful work. An implantation approach would instead need a reproducible supply of suitable muscle, effective delivery, sustained survival, and adequate blood supply within the injured heart. These are requirements inferred from the proposed capability, not findings verified from the full review.

Engineering synthesis: either route must overcome integration at several levels. New tissue must receive adequate perfusion, transmit force through the ventricular wall, and contract in coordination with native myocardium without creating clinically important rhythm disturbances. Demonstrating additional muscle is therefore a separate task from demonstrating useful pumping work, and both are separate from establishing durable patient benefit. Imaging and histology can contribute evidence of tissue formation but cannot alone establish electrical coupling.

current_state.text: In “Molecular gatekeepers of endogenous adult mammalian cardiomyocyte proliferation,” published on 7 April 2025, Tim Koopmans and Eva van Rooij describe post-infarction fibrosis, cardiomyocyte death, and chronic dysfunction as a substantial clinical challenge without an available curative treatment. They also describe the largely lost proliferative capacity of adult mammalian cardiomyocytes. These are statements from a dated review, rather than a complete assessment of every clinical approach through November 2026.

The same review reports successful reactivation of cardiomyocyte cell-cycle induction in preclinical adult-animal models, accompanied by functional recovery after cardiac injury. This provides a biological basis for pursuing regeneration, but does not establish effective human remuscularization. The retained material includes the abstract and key points, with author information, rather than the full review. It does not provide sufficient inspected study detail here to assess individual models, effect sizes, durability, or translation to patients; figure captions and reference titles cannot substitute for those results.

The supplied research attributes several quantitative findings to the 2025 Circulation paper “A Latent Cardiomyocyte Regeneration Potential in Human Heart Disease”: carbon-14-based estimates of approximately 0.5% annual cardiomyocyte renewal in healthy adults, generation rates 18 to 50 times lower in end-stage heart failure, and increased renewal in some hearts unloaded with a ventricular assist device. The source index contains no retained text or artifact for that paper, so these figures and the unloading finding remain reported but unverified within this record. That evidence gap does not show that the findings are false. If confirmed, the unloading observation would be a clue to regenerative potential, rather than proof of a controllable remuscularization treatment.

The supplied material does not establish whether tested human cell products have produced remuscularization, nor does it substantiate the original blanket summary that two decades of cell therapy have failed to do so. It also contains no completed freshness search establishing clinical status as of 1 November 2026. The defensible conclusion is that the retained evidence documents a regenerative goal and preclinical progress, while leaving the human treatment record and subsequent developments unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: in a defined population after substantial myocardial infarction or with an appropriately specified form of systolic heart failure, treatment should produce durable new myocardium and show that it contributes useful contractile work. Imaging and histology, where feasible and ethically obtainable, should establish tissue formation; complementary functional measurements should establish coordinated electrical activation and mechanical contribution. A transient paracrine improvement without new muscle would not satisfy this concept. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical evidence: a randomized comparison against appropriate guideline-directed care should demonstrate a prespecified, clinically important improvement in ventricular function and a reduction in death or heart-failure hospitalization. Ejection fraction could be one functional endpoint, but no universal numerical cutoff is adopted here. The protocol should distinguish durable recovery from short-lived changes and define the clinically meaningful effect before outcomes are known.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed clinical evidence

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and safety boundaries: convincing completion would require independently reproducible benefit, sustained follow-up, and acceptable risks of arrhythmia, inappropriate tissue growth, immune complications where relevant, and delivery-related harm. The treatment should have reproducible manufacturing or delivery and a usable range of doses or treatment conditions. Follow-up duration and acceptable risk thresholds would need prospective justification rather than being assumed.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and safety boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope of the conclusion: trials should specify injury type, disease cause, scar burden, baseline function, and concomitant treatment. Success in one population would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions; it would not prove effectiveness across every cardiomyopathy or literal universality. Failure to stop an ongoing disease process should also be distinguished from failure of the new muscle itself to survive or function.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed scope of the conclusion

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: CLM-05, “Durable organ xenotransplantation at clinical scale,” and CLM-11, “Implantable human-scale organs assembled outside the body,” overlap with this concept as possible routes to restoring cardiac function through replacement. CLM-06 centers on rebuilding muscle within an existing heart; the other entries concern donor-organ replacement or organs assembled outside the body. Engineered cardiac tissue could create a technical connection with CLM-11, but the supplied roster does not define whether that entry includes partial tissue constructs. No comparative claim about patient population size is established.

Roster-based comparison: CLM-04, “Restoration of adult human central nervous system circuitry after injury,” and CLM-15, “Restoration of nephron number in the adult human kidney,” share the broader ambition of rebuilding functional biological structures after adult tissue loss. Their completion requirements remain distinct: coordinated cardiac contraction does not establish restored neural circuitry or new functioning nephrons. CLM-04 is broader than the earlier shorthand of reconnecting a severed spinal cord.

Roster-based comparison: CLM-09, “Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver,” could overlap if genome writing were used to control cardiac regeneration, but remuscularization does not require that particular method, and genome writing alone would not demonstrate muscle restoration. CLM-01, “Programmable antigen-specific immune tolerance,” could be relevant to implanted cells requiring immune acceptance, while CLM-08, “Safe multi-tissue reversal of human biological aging,” could intersect with efforts to alter adult cell state. These are conditional connections inferred from the roster titles, not demonstrated dependencies or grounds for merging the entries.

change_log.change: Preserved CLM-06 and its title while defining the capability around durable restoration of functioning muscle within the existing adult human heart.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent despite gaps in evidence for some supporting assertions.

change_log.change: Integrated endogenous regeneration and implanted-muscle approaches, distinguishing tissue formation, electrical and mechanical integration, and patient benefit.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain what the innovation requires and prevent cell-cycle activity or temporary signaling effects from being treated as completed remuscularization.

change_log.change: Retained the approximately 0.5% annual renewal estimate, the 18-to-50-fold reduction, and the ventricular-unloading observation as explicitly unverified reports.
change_log.reason: The original research supplies these details, but the Circulation source has no retained artifact. Missing evidence warrants qualification rather than deletion or a finding of falsity.

change_log.change: Corrected the Nature Reviews Cardiology attribution to Tim Koopmans and Eva van Rooij and added the supported preclinical adult-animal functional-recovery finding.
change_log.reason: The validated review identifies the authors and reports relevant progress omitted from the earlier narrative.

change_log.change: Preserved the limited access to the review and separated its April 2025 statements from unresolved clinical status in November 2026.
change_log.reason: The retained abstract and key points do not establish the complete human treatment record or subsequent developments.

change_log.change: Removed categorical claims that tested cell products have never remuscularized a human heart and that two decades of cell therapy establish this conclusion.
change_log.reason: The retained evidence does not support those comprehensive clinical assertions.

change_log.change: Corrected the implication that transplantation does not supply working myocardium, removed unsupported population comparisons, and qualified extension to dilated cardiomyopathy.
change_log.reason: Whole-heart replacement supplies working muscle, population reach is unquantified, and ongoing disease could limit the benefit of muscle restoration.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to address functional coupling, durability, reproducibility, safety, and defined patient populations without adopting a numerical ejection-fraction threshold.
change_log.reason: Imaging and histology alone cannot establish electrical integration, and finite demonstrations support bounded clinical claims.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster to clarify related concepts and corrected CLM-04's earlier spinal-cord-only description.
change_log.reason: The roster supplies definitions unavailable to the reviewer, while preserving distinct concepts and avoiding unsupported comparisons.

unresolved_issues: The Circulation paper's identity and findings cannot be verified from retained document content; the renewal estimates, end-stage-failure comparison, and ventricular-unloading results remain unresolved.
The supplied record does not establish the complete history of human cell-product remuscularization or clinical developments through 1 November 2026.
The full Nature Reviews Cardiology review was not available in the retained preview, limiting assessment of individual preclinical studies, effect sizes, methods, durability, and safety.
Eligible patient numbers, comparative reach versus replacement-heart approaches, and effectiveness across different causes of dilated cardiomyopathy are not established.
A future demonstration protocol must specify measurements of electrical and mechanical contribution, follow-up duration, clinically meaningful effects, and acceptable safety boundaries.
The relationship between partial engineered cardiac tissue and CLM-11 remains undefined by the supplied roster title.
